clue.text: First Latin bishop

definitions.meaning: the presiding bishop of the Scottish Episcopal Church

explanation.surface: A question about who was the earliest bishop of the Latin church.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the Latin adjective meaning first; the other is the title of the chief bishop of the Scottish Episcopal Church.

clue.text: Alias Bailey?

parts.note: Donald Bailey designed the Bailey bridge, so he is a bridge-builder, which is the Latin title of Roman high priests

explanation.surface: Asking what other name a man called Bailey goes by.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin title of Roman priests means bridge-maker; Bailey invented the wartime Bailey bridge, so he earns the title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman priestly title literally means bridge-builder, which describes the bridge designer Bailey.

clue.text: Contrariwise, I pronounce myself adult

parts.note: turning that claim to its opposite gives the word for not grown up

explanation.surface: Someone stubbornly declaring they are a grown-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I pronounce myself adult' is I'M MATURE; 'Contrariwise' asks for its opposite, which is spelt with the same letters run together.
explanation.definitionFit: The opposite of being grown up is being childish or not fully developed.

clue.text: Speaker's Lake

definitions.meaning: James Lowther, Speaker of the House of Commons
a lake in the English Lake District

explanation.surface: A question about which lake a speaker owns.
explanation.walkthrough: The Speaker is the chair of the British House of Commons; Lowther took his title from the Lake District lake.
explanation.definitionFit: The Speaker's peerage title and the second-largest lake in the Lake District share the same name.

clue.text: Make a secret of how to cook eggs?

definitions.meaning: to encode a message so outsiders cannot read it
a way of preparing eggs by stirring them in the pan

explanation.surface: A kitchen riddle about keeping a recipe for eggs to oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: To garble a signal so it is secret is one sense; stirring beaten eggs in a pan is the other.

clue.text: "O thou soul of my soul! I shall.. thee again " (Browning)

definitions.text: "O thou soul of my soul! I shall.. thee again " (Browning)

parts.words: O thou soul of my soul! I shall.. thee again
parts.note: a missing-word quotation from Browning's Prospice, where he looks forward to holding his dead wife once more

explanation.surface: A line from Browning's poem Prospice with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots mark the missing word: Browning ends Prospice 'I shall [embrace] thee again, And with God be the rest!'
explanation.definitionFit: The blank is the verb for holding someone tightly in one's arms.

clue.text: All this for one single!

indicators.note: 'this for' asks for one letter of the word to be swapped out and the word one put in its place

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cry that everything here is meant for just one person.
explanation.walkthrough: In ALL, one L is replaced by ONE, giving A-L-ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being solitary or by oneself is being single in the sense of on one's own.

clue.text: Galway sports coat

parts.note: the Galway ... are a famous Irish fox hunt, and a sports jacket is also called by this name

explanation.surface: A tweed jacket from the west of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Galway sports' points to the Galway Blazers, a foxhunt in Ireland; a light sports jacket is a blazer too.
explanation.definitionFit: A club or sports jacket is a blazer, and the Galway hunt's members are the Blazers.

clue.text: Foreshadowing Steven

parts.note: the saying 'coming ... cast their shadows before', with the name Steven rearranged into the answer

explanation.surface: Someone hinting at what will happen to a man named Steven.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'coming events cast their shadows before' makes happenings the things that foreshadow, and the letters of STEVEN can be rearranged to spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Happenings, in the proverb, cast their shadows ahead of them.

clue.text: "You have dancing shoes With soles " (R and J)

definitions.text: "You have dancing shoes With soles " (R and J)

parts.words: You have dancing shoes With soles
parts.note: a missing-word quotation: Romeo, in Romeo and Juliet, tells Mercutio his dancing shoes have quick, light-footed soles

explanation.surface: A line from Romeo and Juliet with one word blanked out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Times puzzles set quotation clues: the printed dash marks the missing word, and the solver supplies it from the play (Act 1, Scene 4).
explanation.definitionFit: The blank in Romeo's line is filled by an adjective meaning quick and agile on the feet.

clue.text: A shoe, as the years go on, is likely to cause damage

parts.note: a sabot is a wooden clog, a kind of shoe
as years pass a person gains age

explanation.surface: A warning that an old shoe wears out and causes harm as time passes.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from French workers said to have thrown their sabots into machinery to wreck it.
explanation.definitionFit: To wreck something deliberately is to sabotage it, so the verb means to cause damage on purpose.

clue.text: Through which Juliet made a sunny appearance

definitions.text: Through which Juliet made a sunny appearance

parts.words: Through which Juliet made a sunny appearance
parts.note: Romeo sees Juliet at an opening above and says 'what light through yonder ... breaks? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun'

explanation.surface: A recollection of the balcony scene in Romeo and Juliet.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo compares Juliet to the sun rising through the opening in the wall above him.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening in a wall that lets light in is what Juliet appears through.

clue.text: Thus " I'll string along with you " or maybe I won't

indicators.note: 'or maybe' offers the letters of the next words in some other possible arrangement

parts.note: taken as written: the letters I, W, O, N, T

explanation.surface: Someone half-promising to go along with a friend, then having second thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or maybe' turns I WON'T into IN TOW; the apostrophe is not a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being pulled along behind someone, as a towed boat is, is what a person who strings along is.

clue.text: Instrument for a performer

parts.note: a tool, and also what a person who carries out (performs) a plan does: the verb sense of the same word

explanation.surface: A musical instrument being chosen for someone on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument' and 'performer' suggest music, but the word means a tool, and as a verb it means to perform or carry out.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool or utensil is an implement, and one who implements a plan performs it.

clue.text: Greet the White Heron from me

indicators.note: 'from me' asks for the clue's word to be rearranged, with the letters coming out in a new order as a greeting from the setter

explanation.surface: A friendly message sending good wishes to a white heron.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is very loose by modern standards: 'from me' asks for GREET rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The egret is a heron, most species white-plumed.

clue.text: "And love to live in sleek " (Milton)

parts.words: And love to live in sleek
parts.note: a missing-word quotation from Milton's L'Allegro, where Love lives in a small hollow of a smiling cheek

explanation.surface: A line from Milton's L'Allegro with one word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash in the printed clue marks the missing word: Milton writes of laughter 'And love to live in [a little hollow] sleek'.
explanation.definitionFit: The line's blank is filled by a word for a small hollow in a cheek or chin.

clue.text: Sam's pick-up?

parts.note: Stanley Holloway's comic monologue has the line 'Sam, Sam, pick up tha' ...', which Sam refuses

explanation.surface: Asking what a man called Sam collects or gives a lift to.
explanation.walkthrough: Stanley Holloway's music-hall monologue about the soldier Sam Small turns on the order to pick up his old firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: The thing Sam is told to pick up in the monologue is his old smooth-bore army gun.

clue.text: All sorts of drink in the cooler

parts.note: liquor is alcoholic drink
ice keeps things cool

explanation.surface: Every kind of drink kept chilled.
explanation.walkthrough: Liquorice Allsorts are a well-known British mixed sweet, so 'All sorts' defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquorice Allsorts are a famous British assortment of black sweets, so the phrase names them.

clue.text: "In the Spring a — iris changes on the burnish'd dove " (Tennyson)

definitions.text: "In the Spring a — iris changes on the burnish'd dove " (Tennyson)

parts.words: In the Spring a — iris changes on the burnish'd dove
parts.note: a missing-word quotation from Tennyson's Locksley Hall: in spring the dove's neck shows brighter colours

explanation.surface: A line from Tennyson's Locksley Hall with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the missing word in Tennyson's line about spring brightening the dove's iridescent plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank needs a comparative adjective meaning brighter or more vivid.

clue.text: Solecisms under the spreading chestnut-tree?

definitions.meaning: Longfellow's village smithy stands under a spreading chestnut tree, where hammers ring loudly on the anvil

explanation.surface: Grammatical errors made beneath a large chestnut tree.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's poem The Village Blacksmith opens 'Under a spreading chestnut tree'; the things that clang there are the hammer blows.
explanation.definitionFit: Embarrassing mistakes are clangers, and so, read literally, are things that clang, like the smith's hammer.

clue.text: Low murmurs from the Jarndyce Library

definitions.text: Low murmurs from the Jarndyce Library

parts.words: Low murmurs from the Jarndyce Library
parts.note: in Dickens's Bleak House Mr Jarndyce calls his private room the Growlery, where he goes to grumble when the wind is in the east

explanation.surface: Quiet whispering coming from a library in a grand house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Library' suggests hushed voices, but Jarndyce's room in Bleak House is named the Growlery, so the low sounds from it are grumblings.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep rumbling grumbles are what the Growlery is named after.

clue.text: No doubt it helps to feather the writer's nest

definitions.text: No doubt it helps to feather the writer's nest

parts.words: No doubt it helps to feather the writer's nest
parts.note: a feather pen earns an author money, and is itself a feather

explanation.surface: A remark that something makes an author wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: To feather one's nest is to grow rich; the writer's tool, a pen made from a feather, both pays the author and is literally a feather.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen cut from a bird's flight feather is the old writing tool, and it is a feather.

clue.text: Shaggy dogs in the cornfield

definitions.meaning: a shock dog was a poodle-like dog with a thick shaggy coat
sheaves of corn stood upright together in a field to dry

explanation.surface: Unkempt dogs loose in a field of corn.
explanation.definitionFit: Old shaggy-coated dogs were called shocks, and stooks of sheaves in a harvest field are shocks too.

clue.text: Lizards from South Africa pursued by the 'ittite

indicators.note: 'pursued by' puts the second piece after the first, following it

parts.note: Uriah the Hittite of the Bible, with his H dropped as the clue drops the H of Hittite

explanation.surface: Lizards from South Africa being chased by an ancient Hittite.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah the Hittite was Bathsheba's husband in the Bible; the apostrophe in ''ittite' shows an aitch dropped, so URIAH loses its H too.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauria is the old scientific name for the group containing lizards.

clue.text: A matter of grave importance for Bradley

definitions.meaning: a stone set up over a grave
Bradley ... is the schoolmaster in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend

explanation.surface: Something seriously important to a man named Bradley.
explanation.definitionFit: A gravestone is what stands at a grave; Bradley's surname in Dickens's novel is the same word.

clue.text: The saint's got everything, including a good seat

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for saint
all is everything

explanation.surface: A saint who has everything, including a fine place to sit.
explanation.walkthrough: A stall is a good seat in a theatre, or a seat in a church choir.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre seat in the front ground-floor section is a stall.

clue.text: Stars beautifully girdled

parts.note: a constellation known for the belt of three bright stars across its middle

explanation.surface: Film stars dressed in elegant belts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'girdled' means belted: the Hunter constellation has a famous belt of three stars.
explanation.definitionFit: The constellation of the Hunter is a group of stars with a well-known belt.

clue.text: Classical component of a juke-box

parts.note: a Greek music hall; also the last five letters of ..., an old American name for a coin jukebox

explanation.surface: Asking which classical record is part of a jukebox's selection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classical' suggests classical music, but it means ancient Greek: the odeon was a Greek hall for music, and it ends the word nickelodeon, a coin-operated jukebox.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek roofed theatre for music is the odeon, and the word is the last part of nickelodeon.

clue.text: Dairy cat in a supporting role

indicators.note: 'in' here signals that the letters of the words before it are to be found rearranged within the answer

explanation.surface: A cat on a dairy farm given a minor part in a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' turns DAIRY CAT into CARYATID; 'supporting role' suggests acting, but the figure literally holds up a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A carved female figure used as a column holds up the building, so her role is to bear weight.

clue.text: Can you make out the Minister?

definitions.meaning: to discern or guess something by insight
a clergyman, a minister of religion

explanation.surface: A question whether one can recognise a government minister.
explanation.definitionFit: To guess by intuition is to divine; a churchman or theologian is called a divine.

clue.text: There's a scheme in the bishop's office to get a flier

indicators.note: 'in' says the plan goes inside the word for the bishop's office

parts.note: a bishop's see is his seat and the district he governs
a plan is a scheme

explanation.surface: Someone plotting inside a bishop's office to get a pilot or a leaflet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flier' suggests a person, but it is a plane that lands on water.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft is a flying machine, a flier, and this one lands on water.

clue.text: Mrs. Battle's favourite suit

parts.note: Charles Lamb's essay Mrs Battle's Opinions on Whist describes an old lady devoted to cards and her favoured suit

explanation.surface: A question about a woman's favourite outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' suggests clothes, but Lamb's Mrs Battle was a whist player, and the suit is a card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the four card suits, the red one marked with love symbols is the one she preferred.
